tasks.short: Replenish demonstration shelves and record stock movements.

steps.what: Inspect shelves and identify replenishment needs.
Collect the required products from backroom stock.
Place products safely, rotate stock, and straighten the display.
Enter replenished quantities and stock exceptions in the {OPS_SYSTEM}.

tasks.design: Configure a replenishment view and barcode entry in the {OPS_SYSTEM}, using existing item locations and stock rules. The demonstrator confirms actual quantities during replenishment; the same entry creates the stock movement record and flags exceptions for the store supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Physical handling dominates. Separate shelf checks and later quantity entry create small administrative delays, but automation cannot remove the lifting and placement.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing scanning and replenishment settings may cover the administrative work. AI-assisted configuration or small extensions can reduce setup effort; no model is needed at runtime.
tasks.still_hard: Stock records may disagree with shelves. Safe handling, damaged packaging, expiry checks, and access to backroom stock remain physical work.
tasks.human_edge: Notice unsafe placement, damage, and customer disruption while keeping the display attractive.
tasks.altitude: The week contains slightly less quantity entry and searching. Physical replenishment remains the task, and no new decision rights are assumed.

reach.role: first-line supervisor of retail sales workers
reach.learn: Stock accuracy, replenishment thresholds, and how to distinguish a temporary display shortage from a supply problem.

evidence.claim: Shelf replenishment remains physical; scanning and stock rules can reduce recording work. The time estimates are planning assumptions.

assumptions: The venue uses an {OPS_SYSTEM} for stock movements and gives demonstrators limited access.
The {OPS_SYSTEM} supports barcode entry and replenishment views through configuration.
Physical handling outweighs communication, despite the supplied kind prior; the means prior supports predominantly in-person work.
The solution records stock movements without introducing employee performance scoring.
unknowns: Whether demonstrators can access venue stock records.
Whether barcode entry, shelf locations, and replenishment thresholds are already configured.
Whether replenishment quantities require recording or only exceptions do.
Whether employee consultation under national rules applies to the proposed activity logging.
research_questions: Which stock entries duplicate information already captured during replenishment?
Can existing configuration support the workflow without a separate application?
new_work: Resolve discrepancies between recorded stock and shelf counts.
Maintain item locations and replenishment thresholds.
Check failed or duplicate stock movement entries.

tasks.short: Present product information and answer audience questions using approved demonstration materials.

steps.what: Find current product facts, prices, and approved media in the {DOCS}.
Assemble slides, charts, and clips for the audience and session.
Check the presentation for accurate claims, prices, and audience suitability.
Deliver the presentation and adapt the explanation to audience reactions.
Answer questions and identify any answers requiring specialist follow-up.

tasks.design: Keep versioned facts and approved presentation modules in the {DOCS}. A deterministic generator selects modules from the session brief, assembles the presentation, and checks dates and required notices; the demonstrator approves it before use and handles the live conversation.
tasks.previous_blocker: Materials were reusable, but scattered versions and manual assembly made each session require preparation.
tasks.enabler_now: Templates, metadata, and simple assembly rules already support this approach. AI-assisted coding makes a small generator cheaper to build; runtime generation needs no model when approved modules cover the session.
tasks.still_hard: Maintaining accurate source material and judging what an audience understands. Unusual questions still require product knowledge or specialist follow-up.
tasks.human_edge: Read the room, make the demonstration credible, and explain limitations honestly.

ambition.what: Short introductory sessions for first-time buyers with little product knowledge.

tasks.altitude: Preparation takes less of the week, leaving room for introductory sessions and better follow-up. The demonstrator chooses approved modules and pacing; authority to invent claims or change prices does not expand.

reach.task: Explain product suitability and limitations during a demonstration.
reach.learn: Translate specifications into practical examples and recognise questions that need technical verification.

evidence.claim: Approved modules and templates can automate presentation assembly while live explanation remains human. Savings depend on source quality and reuse.

assumptions: Most sessions can use approved modules rather than newly written claims.
The demonstrator checks each assembled presentation before public use.
Live delivery remains dominant, but preparation receives more time than the supplied means prior suggests.
The design does not record audiences or collect identifiable audience profiles.
unknowns: Whether approved claims, prices, and media have reliable owners and version dates.
Which audience types need different presentation modules.
Whether media rights allow reuse in each venue.
Which claims require specialist approval beyond the demonstrator's existing authority.
research_questions: How many recent presentations could have been assembled entirely from approved modules?
Does the {DOCS} already support reusable presentation templates well enough to avoid custom code?
new_work: Maintain approved modules and their expiry dates.
Route unanswered questions and add verified answers to the source material.

tasks.short: Train demonstrators to explain products accurately and deliver effective live demonstrations.

steps.what: Review product changes and identify the trainees' learning needs.
Prepare approved examples, practice exercises, and assessment checklists.
Explain the product and coach trainees through practice demonstrations.
Observe a demonstration and decide readiness or further practice needs.
Record the outcome and assign follow-up learning in the {LMS}.

tasks.design: Use a deterministic generator to assemble training packs from approved modules in the {DOCS}, with trainer approval before use. Configure the {LMS} so the trainer's readiness decision creates the training record and assigns agreed follow-up learning without duplicate entry.
tasks.previous_blocker: Coaching is personal, so the surrounding preparation and recording often stayed manual too. Reusable exercises were not consistently separated from session-specific material.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing learning assignments and document templates cover much of the work. AI-assisted coding can connect the remaining fields without introducing automated assessment.
tasks.still_hard: Recognising unsafe technique, misplaced confidence, and difficulty responding to customers. A checklist supports the trainer but cannot establish readiness alone.
tasks.human_edge: Build confidence through specific feedback and judge whether someone can demonstrate safely and answer honestly.

ambition.what: A targeted refresher clinic for demonstrators returning after a product change.

tasks.altitude: The lead demonstrator spends less time assembling packs and copying outcomes, with more room for targeted coaching. Existing readiness authority stays with the trainer; no new employment decision rights are assumed.

reach.role: first-line supervisor of retail sales workers
reach.task: Coach staff and assign appropriate demonstration duties.
reach.learn: Use consistent observation criteria, give useful feedback, and recognise when a readiness concern needs supervisor involvement.

evidence.claim: Training-pack assembly and learning assignments can be automated while live coaching and readiness decisions remain human.
GDPR applies to identifiable training records. Access, retention, and consultation requirements under national rules need local assessment.

assumptions: The company uses an {LMS}, but trainers still prepare materials and enter practical assessment outcomes manually.
The trainer has existing authority to determine demonstration readiness.
The design uses no trainee recording, model scoring, or automated employment decisions.
In-person practice and observation remain the large majority of task time, consistent with the supplied priors.
unknowns: Whether practical assessments and follow-up assignments are already connected in the {LMS}.
Whether training records affect deployment, pay, or formal employment decisions.
Which roles may see individual feedback and how long it is retained.
Whether national rules require employee consultation and how long that process takes.
research_questions: Which training materials can be reused without losing the product-specific practice trainees need?
Can existing {LMS} configuration remove duplicate entry without an integration?
new_work: Maintain exercises and assessment criteria when products change.
Resolve failed learning assignments and incorrect training records.
Review access and retention settings for individual feedback.

tasks.short: Turn customer reactions and demonstration experience into product or service improvement recommendations.

steps.what: Notice recurring questions, usage difficulties, and objections during demonstrations.
Write brief examples and context in field notes.
Compare notes and group repeated issues in a working table.

loop.input: A fixed batch of field notes with note identifiers, product identifiers, and session dates.
loop.output: Proposed issue groups with linked note identifiers and representative excerpts.
loop.check: Validate note identifiers and exact excerpts automatically. The demonstrator checks groupings, missed issues, and misleading merges before accepting the table.
loop.stop: One classification pass and one repair pass per batch. Unresolved notes remain ungrouped for manual review; no automatic escalation or publication.
loop.why_not_simpler: The same problem is described in varied free text. Product fields and fixed categories help, but keyword rules alone miss paraphrases and context.

steps.what: Choose a useful improvement and write a supported recommendation.
Discuss the recommendation with the product manager and agree the next action.

tasks.design: Configure a short field-note form in the {WORKFLOW} and keep the evidence in the {DOCS}. A bounded classification loop proposes issue groups with source excerpts; deterministic code counts distinct sessions and fills a recommendation template after review. The demonstrator chooses the recommendation, and the product manager approves any resulting product change or trial.
tasks.previous_blocker: Anecdotes were scattered and costly to compare. Structured forms alone could not reliably group different descriptions of the same difficulty.
tasks.enabler_now: A bounded text-classification loop can propose groups while preserving the source notes. Forms, counts, templates, and follow-up tracking remain deterministic.
tasks.still_hard: Demonstration audiences are a biased sample. Repeated comments do not establish market demand, root cause, or the commercial value of a change.
tasks.human_edge: Distinguish a genuine product problem from presentation confusion and argue for a practical improvement without overstating the evidence.

ambition.what: A weekly choice of one product-instruction improvement to recommend for a small trial.

tasks.altitude: The demonstrator brings traceable examples to a regular improvement discussion instead of rebuilding an anecdotal case. They choose which recommendation to advance; product changes and trial approval remain with the product manager, with no new formal authority assumed.

reach.task: Prioritise recurring customer objections for product feedback.
reach.learn: Separate frequency from severity, recognise sample bias, and define a small trial with a clear success measure.

evidence.claim: Forms, source-linked grouping, counts, and templates can reduce feedback administration. This digest provides no direct demonstrator deployment case.
Verint Wrap Up Bot documents adjacent text-to-record capability through call summaries written to a CRM; it does not establish field-note clustering performance.
EU AI Act Article 4 requires AI literacy for relevant staff using the classification loop.
Identifiable customer or employee information in feedback remains subject to GDPR; national rules may affect employee consultation.

assumptions: Demonstrators currently keep brief notes and sometimes compare issues in a working table.
The time split includes observation specifically used for recommendations, not the whole demonstration counted again.
Direct observation and discussion dominate, while explicit evidence preparation takes more time than the supplied means prior suggests.
The form avoids customer names and unnecessary personal details; incidental personal data needs controlled handling.
The design uses no ambient recording or employee performance scoring.
unknowns: How much usable feedback exists and whether notes have consistent product and session identifiers.
Whether feedback includes personal or commercially sensitive information.
Whether a working table is currently used or comparison happens entirely in conversation.
Who may approve a trial and what budget or operational limits apply.
Whether national rules require employee consultation for the proposed collection and processing.
research_questions: Do fixed issue categories cover most notes well enough to avoid a model loop?
How often does proposed grouping merge distinct problems or miss important isolated incidents?
Which trial measures distinguish clearer product instructions from changes in audience or venue?
new_work: Review proposed groups against their source notes.
Keep isolated but serious issues visible.
Remove unnecessary personal details from notes.
Maintain issue categories and check classification quality after product changes.
Track approved trials and return outcomes to demonstrators.

role.altitude: The role remains centred on physical demonstrations, customer conversations, and coaching. Less preparation and duplicate recording creates room for targeted sessions and stronger improvement proposals; pricing, product, and employment decision rights do not automatically expand.
reach: First-line supervisor of retail sales workers: replenishment planning and practical staff coaching.
Sales engineer: accurate explanations of product suitability and limitations.
Sales manager: evidence-based prioritisation of customer objections.
skills_to_grow: Maintain approved product facts and reusable demonstration materials.
Capture concise observations without unnecessary personal data.
Check grouped feedback against original evidence.
Coach through observation and specific feedback.
Design small trials and interpret results without overstating them.
Use model-assisted tools with appropriate AI literacy.
role.ambitious_version: A demonstrator who delivers trusted live experiences, runs targeted refresher clinics, and regularly brings source-backed product-instruction improvements to decision makers.
